screens.title: Abstract Classes and Abstract Methods
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll learn how abstract classes and abstract methods let you define required behavior for a family of related classes while still providing shared implementation. An abstract class is a class you cannot instantiate. You mark it with the abstract keyword and use it as a blueprint. Abstract methods declare a signature but no body; they say, in effect, “any concrete subclass must implement this.” This combination is powerful when some behavior is common across subclasses but other behavior must vary by type. For example, a Shape class can store a color and provide a concrete displayColor method, while leaving calculateArea and draw as abstract methods that each concrete shape implements. You’ll see how this prevents calling meaningless defaults and how the compiler enforces the contract at compile time. We also cover the common pitfalls: trying to new an abstract class, or forgetting to implement all abstract methods in a concrete subclass. By the end of the chapter you will be able to design an abstract superclass, implement concrete subclasses, and reason about when an abstract class is the correct design choice in place of a plain class.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Abstract Classes
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Abstract Classes and Abstract Methods

Use abstract classes to define a required interface for subclasses while sharing concrete code. Abstract methods declare what must be implemented; abstract classes cannot be instantiated. This pattern enforces design contracts early, at compile time.

In this lesson
You will: define abstract classes and methods, implement them in concrete subclasses, and recognize compile-time enforcement and common mistakes.
Why it matters
It prevents incomplete objects and ensures that essential behaviors are always provided by concrete subclasses.
Explore Key Topics
Abstract vs Concrete
When a superclass has required behaviors but no meaningful default implementation.
Abstract Methods
Signatures without bodies that force subclasses to implement them.
Design Contract
Compile-time enforcement of required behavior across an inheritance hierarchy.
Shape Hierarchy (concept)
Blueprint + concrete parts
Abstract Superclass
Shape
color, displayColor() — concrete; calculateArea() — abstract
Concrete Subclass
Circle
Implements calculateArea() and draw()
Concrete Subclass
Rectangle
Implements calculateArea() and draw()
Quick note
Abstract classes can also include fields and constructors. They are partial templates: some behavior supplied, some left required for subclasses.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives will guide your work with abstract classes and abstract methods. First, you will be able to define what an abstract class and an abstract method are, and explain their purpose as a design blueprint. That means recognizing that an abstract class cannot be instantiated and that abstract methods have signatures only. Second, you will identify scenarios where choosing an abstract class is the right design: when a family of classes shares common data or helper behavior but each concrete class must provide a specific implementation for certain methods. Third, you will implement abstract classes and their abstract methods using the abstract keyword, creating constructors and concrete helpers inside the abstract class while forcing subclasses to finish required behaviors. Finally, you will understand the rules for extending abstract classes, including that a concrete subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods or itself become abstract. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding by inspecting an inheritance hierarchy and spotting whether required methods are implemented.

screens.title: How you'll demonstrate competence
screens.narratorSegment: To verify competence, you’ll complete hands-on checks that map to the objectives. First, inspect an inheritance hierarchy and identify whether the superclass should be abstract because one or more methods lack a meaningful default. Second, write an abstract class that combines fields, a constructor, and one or more concrete helper methods, plus at least one abstract method that subclasses must implement. Third, create concrete subclasses that correctly override and implement every inherited abstract method; the test is that each concrete subclass compiles without being declared abstract. Fourth, reflect on design choices by comparing an abstract superclass to a plain concrete class: when does mixing shared implementation and required methods improve clarity and reduce duplication? Each milestone is intentionally practical: compiling code, running simple output, and spotting common mistakes. These steps ensure you do not only understand the definition but can apply it and verify behavior during development.

screens.title: What is an abstract class?
screens.narratorSegment: An abstract class is a class declared with the abstract keyword that you cannot instantiate. Think of it as a partial template: it can hold fields, constructors, and concrete methods that provide shared behavior, but it can also declare abstract methods without bodies to require subclass-specific implementations. The core idea is that the abstract class expresses a contract and shares common code at the same time. For example, a Shape class might store a color and implement displayColor, while leaving calculateArea and draw undefined because their behavior depends on the specific shape. That mix is what distinguishes an abstract class from a plain concrete superclass. A common misconception is to assume abstract classes must be empty shells; they are not. You can put useful helpers, default logic, and shared state in them. Another misconception is to assume they are only for polymorphism; while they enable polymorphism, their main job is enforcing that concrete subclasses supply essential behavior. A quick rule: if a superclass has a method with no meaningful default implementation, make it abstract so subclasses must implement it. Reflect: when you find repeated code across subclasses but one method varies by type, an abstract class often reduces duplication while guaranteeing required behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is an abstract class?
Definition
A class declared abstract that cannot be instantiated and may contain both abstract and concrete members.
Analogy: a blueprint for buildings that also includes some pre-built fixtures. The blueprint cannot be lived in directly, but it defines required rooms and shared plumbing.
When to use: shared fields and helpers, plus required methods implemented by subclasses.
Key Takeaway

Use an abstract class to combine a contract with reusable implementation so subclasses must provide type-specific behavior.

Concrete example: Shape
Shape (abstract)
  • Field: color
  • Concrete: displayColor()
  • Abstract: calculateArea(), draw()
Why this matters
If calculateArea were implemented with a meaningless default, calls through a Shape reference could produce wrong results or runtime surprises. Making it abstract enforces correct implementations in every concrete subclass.

screens.title: What is an abstract method?
screens.narratorSegment: An abstract method is a method declaration without an implementation. You declare it with the abstract keyword and end the declaration with a semicolon. The effect is simple and important: it creates a contract that any concrete subclass must fulfill by providing a method body. This is different from a concrete method where the superclass provides behavior directly. Abstract methods are often used when the superclass cannot provide a meaningful, type-independent implementation. For example, calculateArea on a generic Shape cannot sensibly compute an area because the formula depends on the specific geometry. Declaring calculateArea as abstract forces Circle, Rectangle and any other concrete shapes to implement the correct formula. A common misconception is that abstract methods must be public; in practice they can be protected or public depending on the intended visibility, but they cannot be private since private methods cannot be overridden by subclasses. Also remember: if a class contains at least one abstract method, the class itself must be declared abstract. This rule keeps the compiler consistent: a class with incomplete behavior is not instantiable until those incompletions are resolved in subclasses.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Abstract Method
Abstract Method — concept
A declaration with no body. It creates a programming contract that concrete subclasses must implement. Use it when the superclass cannot provide a useful default.
Common misconceptions
  • They are empty helpers — false: they intentionally require work from subclasses.
  • They must be private — false: private methods cannot be overridden, so abstract methods are typically public or protected.
Key Takeaway

Use abstract methods to require subclass-specific logic while keeping common code in the superclass.

Signature example (visual)
public abstract double calculateArea();
Notice the lack of a method body and the semicolon ending the declaration. This single line enforces that concrete subclasses must implement calculateArea.
Visibility note
Choose public or protected based on whether you expect calls from other packages or just subclasses. The core rule remains: abstract method, no body, required override.

screens.title: Rules for abstract classes and subclasses
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few concrete rules that govern abstract classes and their subclasses. First, if a class contains at least one abstract method, the class itself must be declared abstract. Second, you cannot create an instance of an abstract class; the compiler rejects expressions like creating a new Shape directly. Third, an abstract class may include concrete methods, fields, and constructors. Those members are useful for shared behavior and state. Fourth, a concrete subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods. If it does not, that subclass must itself be declared abstract, deferring implementation further down the hierarchy. These rules enforce that no concrete type can exist with missing essential behavior. A practical process for working with an abstract superclass is: design the contract first—list required abstract methods—then add shared fields and helpers, then implement concrete subclasses and compile early to reveal missing implementations. A common misconception is that an abstract subclass can omit constructors; constructors behave normally. Another pitfall is expecting runtime errors for missing methods; in fact the compiler prevents incomplete concrete classes, catching problems earlier. This compile-time enforcement is what makes abstract classes a reliable design tool.

keyIdea.title: Compiler rules
keyIdea.text: Abstract methods force declaration of the class as abstract, prevent instantiation, and require concrete subclasses to implement all abstract members.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Rules & Compiler
Process: design to compile
  1. Decide which methods must be implemented by every subtype and declare them abstract.
  2. Add shared fields, helpers, and a constructor to the abstract class where appropriate.
  3. Create concrete subclasses and implement every inherited abstract method.
  4. Compile; if a concrete subclass still declares an abstract method, the compiler requires the subclass to be declared abstract or implement the method.
Misconception check: you will not get a runtime exception for missing methods; you will get a compile-time error that prevents incomplete concrete classes from compiling.
Rule Example
Attempting Shape myShape = new Shape("Blue"); results in a compile-time error: Cannot instantiate abstract class.
Concrete helper
An abstract class can still provide working methods like displayColor() so subclasses reuse common implementation rather than duplicating code.
Common mistake
Forgetting to implement all abstract methods in a concrete subclass will make the code fail to compile until resolved.

screens.title: Shape: abstract superclass code
screens.narratorSegment: Let's read the Shape superclass to see how abstract classes combine concrete and abstract members. The Shape class stores a color field and provides a constructor to set it. It also implements displayColor, a concrete helper that every subclass can call. Critically, it declares calculateArea and draw as abstract methods — they have signatures but no implementation. This design forces every concrete subclass to provide a correct area calculation and a draw behavior. Notice the rule: the class contains abstract methods, so it must be declared abstract. A common learner mistake is to try to instantiate Shape; the compiler disallows it because the class is incomplete. Another oversight is to expect default behavior when a subclass forgets to override an abstract method; instead the compiler will require fixes before you can run the program. Walkthroughs like this clarify separation of responsibility: Shape shares common state and helpers while delegating geometric specifics to subclasses. Now examine the code visually and compare it to your mental model: fields and helpers in the superclass; concrete formulas in each subtype. Shape: abstract superclass code means shape provides shared state and helpers and declares required abstract methods that each concrete shape must implement.. In practical terms, read the shape class that mixes fields, constructor, concrete and abstract methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Shape provides shared state and helpers and declares required abstract methods that each concrete shape must implement.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Shape superclass
Abstract Shape (readable code)
<!-- Java code block -->
<!-- escaped for HTML -->
abstract class Shape {
  String color;

  public Shape(String color) {
    this.color = color;
  }

  public void displayColor() {
    System.out.println("Shape color: " + this.color);
  }

  public abstract double calculateArea();

  public abstract void draw();
}
This code shows a constructor, a concrete helper, and two abstract methods. The abstract declarations are the contract that concrete shapes must implement.
Concrete example explained
displayColor uses the shared color field so every subclass inherits a correct way to display its color without reimplementing the method.
Design tip
Put behavior that truly applies to all subclasses in the abstract class and leave variable behavior abstract.
Check your understanding

If a method is meaningful across all shapes, implement it in Shape; otherwise make it abstract so subclasses provide the right behavior.

screens.title: Circle and Rectangle: concrete subclasses
screens.narratorSegment: Now look at concrete subclasses that implement the abstract methods declared in Shape. Circle stores a radius and implements calculateArea by computing pi times radius squared. Rectangle stores width and height and implements calculateArea by multiplying width and height. Both classes override draw and provide behavior that references the shared color field inherited from Shape. These concrete classes are complete: they implement every inherited abstract method and therefore can be instantiated. A common mistake is to forget the @Override annotation; the code still compiles if the method signatures match, but using @Override helps catch signature mismatches early. Another common error is mismatching types or forgetting to call super when necessary for initialization; here subclasses call the Shape constructor with super to set color. Reviewing these implementations shows the cooperative design: Shape supplies the shared parts and the subclasses supply the specifics. Practically, you will test these classes by instantiating them, calling displayColor, draw, and calculateArea, then exercising polymorphism by treating them as Shape references in an array or collection. keyIdea.text: Concrete subclasses must implement every abstract method and may reuse shared fields and helpers from the abstract superclass.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Subclasses
Circle (concrete)
<!-- Circle implementation -->
class Circle extends Shape {
  double radius;

  public Circle(String color, double radius) {
    super(color);
    this.radius = radius;
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateArea() {
    return Math.PI * radius * radius;
  }

  @Override
  public void draw() {
    System.out.println("Drawing a " + color + " circle with radius " + radius);
  }
}
Rectangle (concrete)
<!-- Rectangle implementation -->
class Rectangle extends Shape {
  double width;
  double height;

  public Rectangle(String color, double width, double height) {
    super(color);
    this.width = width;
    this.height = height;
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateArea() {
    return width * height;
  }

  @Override
  public void draw() {
    System.out.println("Drawing a " + color + " rectangle with width " + width + " and height " + height);
  }
}
Practical test
Instantiate concrete subclasses, call displayColor, draw, and calculateArea to verify correct behavior and reuse of shared code from Shape.

screens.title: Polymorphism with abstract classes
screens.narratorSegment: Abstract classes enable polymorphism by providing a common reference type for different concrete implementations. For example, you can store Circle and Rectangle objects in an array of Shape. When you call draw or calculateArea on each Shape reference, the JVM dispatches to the concrete implementation supplied by each object. This makes code more flexible: you can write algorithms that operate on Shape without knowing the specific subclass. An important practical point is that compile-time checking still applies to method availability: the methods you call on a Shape reference must be declared in the Shape class, either as concrete or abstract. The benefit is clear: you get a single A P I to iterate and perform common operations while allowing each subtype to specialize the behavior. A common misconception is thinking polymorphism hides differences — it does not; concrete behavior is preserved at runtime. Also remember the earlier rule: you cannot instantiate Shape directly, but you can create an array or collection typed to Shape and populate it with concrete subclass instances. Consider performance and clarity when designing such hierarchies; use abstract classes when you need shared state plus required methods across the family.

keyIdea.text: Use the abstract superclass as a reference type to treat diverse implementations uniformly while preserving specific runtime behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Polymorphism
Polymorphic usage
You can hold different concrete shapes in a Shape[] and call abstract methods through the Shape type. The runtime will dispatch to each object's implementation.
Example: Shape[] shapes = {new Circle(...), new Rectangle(...)}; then loop calling draw() and calculateArea(). This pattern decouples algorithms from concrete implementations.
Key Takeaway

Polymorphism plus abstract contracts lets you write general code that relies on subtype-specific behavior implemented where it belongs.

Architecture: runtime dispatch
Compile-time check
Methods called on Shape must be declared in Shape.
Runtime behavior
The actual implementation executed is the one provided by the concrete object stored in the Shape reference.
Misconception check: Polymorphism does not remove differences between types — it provides a uniform way to invoke behavior while preserving concrete implementation details.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: Two mistakes appear frequently when learners work with abstract classes. First, attempting to instantiate an abstract class directly. The code new Shape("Blue") will not compile, and you will see a compile-time error stating that you cannot instantiate an abstract class. The fix is to instantiate a concrete subclass such as new Circle("Red", 5.0) instead, or make the subclass implement the missing abstract methods. Second, forgetting to implement all inherited abstract methods in a concrete subclass. If you omit calculateArea or draw in a subclass, the compiler will force you to either implement them or declare the subclass abstract. A frequent related oversight is mismatching method signatures: if you misname a method or change parameter types, your method will not override the abstract declaration, and the compiler will still require an implementation. Use the @Override annotation as a defensive measure so the compiler checks your intent. Finally, another misconception is expecting runtime checks; instead, Java prefers compile-time safety here. The compiler catches these problems early so you can correct them before running the program. Test by compiling after each change to isolate the exact missing implementation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Common mistakes
Mistake: Instantiating abstract class
Attempting to create a new instance of an abstract class produces a compile-time error: Cannot instantiate abstract class. Fix by instantiating a concrete subclass or by providing implementations for abstract methods in a concrete subclass.
Mistake: Missing implementations
If a concrete subclass does not implement all abstract methods, the compiler requires the subclass to be declared abstract. Use the compiler message to find the missing method signatures and implement them.
Pro tip
Annotate methods with @Override to ensure signatures match and to catch accidental mismatches at compile time.

screens.title: When to choose an abstract class
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing an abstract class is a design decision that depends on needs for shared state and required behavior. Use an abstract class when related types share fields, helper methods, or constructors that you want to implement once and reuse. If every subtype must implement a particular method but also needs access to common fields or utilities, an abstract class provides both the contract and the shared implementation. The chapter contrasts this with a plain concrete class, which can be instantiated and therefore must fully implement all behavior; if a method cannot have a sensible default, a concrete class is the wrong choice. The text also emphasizes that abstract classes are ideal when you need a mixture of provided behavior and required overrides. A common misconception is to overuse abstract classes for unrelated types — instead, prefer abstraction only for closely related classes that logically share state and behavior. Reflect with this rule of thumb: if you find yourself duplicating code across subclasses and also needing to force certain methods to be implemented, an abstract class is often the correct pattern.

keyIdea.text: Create an abstract PaymentProcessor with shared logging and concrete subclasses that implement processPayment for each method.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › PaymentProcessor
Starter abstract class
<!-- PaymentProcessor starter -->
abstract class PaymentProcessor {
  String transactionId;
  double amount;

  public PaymentProcessor(String transactionId, double amount) {
    this.transactionId = transactionId;
    this.amount = amount;
  }

  public void logTransaction() {
    System.out.println("Logging transaction " + transactionId + " for amount " + amount);
  }

  public abstract boolean processPayment();
}
Concrete processors (examples)
<!-- CreditCardProcessor & PayPalProcessor -->
class CreditCardProcessor extends PaymentProcessor {
  String cardNumber;

  public CreditCardProcessor(String transactionId, double amount, String cardNumber) {
    super(transactionId, amount);
    this.cardNumber = cardNumber;
  }

  @Override
  public boolean processPayment() {
    System.out.println("Processing credit card " + cardNumber + " for " + amount);
    return true;
  }
}

class PayPalProcessor extends PaymentProcessor {
  String paypalEmail;

  public PayPalProcessor(String transactionId, double amount, String paypalEmail) {
    super(transactionId, amount);
    this.paypalEmail = paypalEmail;
  }

  @Override
  public boolean processPayment() {
    System.out.println("Processing PayPal payment for " + paypalEmail + " for " + amount);
    return true;
  }
}
Try this
Instantiate each processor, call logTransaction and processPayment, and confirm shared logging and different processing messages appear as expected.

screens.title: Compile-time checks and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When a subclass fails to implement an abstract method or when you try to instantiate an abstract class, the compiler gives clear feedback. For instantiation, you will see a message indicating that the abstract class cannot be instantiated. For missing implementations, the compiler reports which methods are not implemented in the concrete class. The correct workflow is to read the compiler message, open the indicated subclass, and add the missing method implementations with the correct signature. Using @Override helps detect accidental signature mismatches that would otherwise be treated as new methods. If you intentionally want a subclass to remain incomplete, declare it abstract and defer implementation further down the hierarchy. Another helpful strategy is to compile early and often while building the hierarchy: create the abstract class first, declare the abstract methods, then add subclasses incrementally and implement required methods as they are reported by the compiler. This process turns compiler errors into a guided checklist. As a reflective question, consider how this compile-time safety influences your confidence when changing shared code in the abstract superclass. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll learn how abstract classes and abstract methods let you define required behavior for a family of related classes while still providing shared implementation. An abstract class is a class you cannot instantiate. You mark it with the abstract keyword and use it as a blueprint. Abstract methods declare a signature but no body; they say, in effect, “any concrete subclass must implement this.” This combination is powerful when some behavior is common across subclasses but other behavior must vary by type. For example, a Shape class can store a color and provide a concrete displayColor method, while leaving calculateArea and draw as abstract methods that each concrete shape implements. You’ll see how this prevents calling meaningless defaults and how the compiler enforces the contract at compile time. We also cover the common pitfalls: trying to new an abstract class, or forgetting to implement all abstract methods in a concrete subclass. By the end of the chapter you will be able to design an abstract superclass, implement concrete subclasses, and reason about when an abstract class is the correct design choice in place of a plain class.

These objectives will guide your work with abstract classes and abstract methods. First, you will be able to define what an abstract class and an abstract method are, and explain their purpose as a design blueprint. That means recognizing that an abstract class cannot be instantiated and that abstract methods have signatures only. Second, you will identify scenarios where choosing an abstract class is the right design: when a family of classes shares common data or helper behavior but each concrete class must provide a specific implementation for certain methods. Third, you will implement abstract classes and their abstract methods using the abstract keyword, creating constructors and concrete helpers inside the abstract class while forcing subclasses to finish required behaviors. Finally, you will understand the rules for extending abstract classes, including that a concrete subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods or itself become abstract. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding by inspecting an inheritance hierarchy and spotting whether required methods are implemented.

To verify competence, you’ll complete hands-on checks that map to the objectives. First, inspect an inheritance hierarchy and identify whether the superclass should be abstract because one or more methods lack a meaningful default. Second, write an abstract class that combines fields, a constructor, and one or more concrete helper methods, plus at least one abstract method that subclasses must implement. Third, create concrete subclasses that correctly override and implement every inherited abstract method; the test is that each concrete subclass compiles without being declared abstract. Fourth, reflect on design choices by comparing an abstract superclass to a plain concrete class: when does mixing shared implementation and required methods improve clarity and reduce duplication? Each milestone is intentionally practical: compiling code, running simple output, and spotting common mistakes. These steps ensure you do not only understand the definition but can apply it and verify behavior during development.

An abstract class is a class declared with the abstract keyword that you cannot instantiate. Think of it as a partial template: it can hold fields, constructors, and concrete methods that provide shared behavior, but it can also declare abstract methods without bodies to require subclass-specific implementations. The core idea is that the abstract class expresses a contract and shares common code at the same time. For example, a Shape class might store a color and implement displayColor, while leaving calculateArea and draw undefined because their behavior depends on the specific shape. That mix is what distinguishes an abstract class from a plain concrete superclass. A common misconception is to assume abstract classes must be empty shells; they are not. You can put useful helpers, default logic, and shared state in them. Another misconception is to assume they are only for polymorphism; while they enable polymorphism, their main job is enforcing that concrete subclasses supply essential behavior. A quick rule: if a superclass has a method with no meaningful default implementation, make it abstract so subclasses must implement it. Reflect: when you find repeated code across subclasses but one method varies by type, an abstract class often reduces duplication while guaranteeing required behavior.

An abstract method is a method declaration without an implementation. You declare it with the abstract keyword and end the declaration with a semicolon. The effect is simple and important: it creates a contract that any concrete subclass must fulfill by providing a method body. This is different from a concrete method where the superclass provides behavior directly. Abstract methods are often used when the superclass cannot provide a meaningful, type-independent implementation. For example, calculateArea on a generic Shape cannot sensibly compute an area because the formula depends on the specific geometry. Declaring calculateArea as abstract forces Circle, Rectangle and any other concrete shapes to implement the correct formula. A common misconception is that abstract methods must be public; in practice they can be protected or public depending on the intended visibility, but they cannot be private since private methods cannot be overridden by subclasses. Also remember: if a class contains at least one abstract method, the class itself must be declared abstract. This rule keeps the compiler consistent: a class with incomplete behavior is not instantiable until those incompletions are resolved in subclasses.

There are a few concrete rules that govern abstract classes and their subclasses. First, if a class contains at least one abstract method, the class itself must be declared abstract. Second, you cannot create an instance of an abstract class; the compiler rejects expressions like creating a new Shape directly. Third, an abstract class may include concrete methods, fields, and constructors. Those members are useful for shared behavior and state. Fourth, a concrete subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods. If it does not, that subclass must itself be declared abstract, deferring implementation further down the hierarchy. These rules enforce that no concrete type can exist with missing essential behavior. A practical process for working with an abstract superclass is: design the contract first—list required abstract methods—then add shared fields and helpers, then implement concrete subclasses and compile early to reveal missing implementations. A common misconception is that an abstract subclass can omit constructors; constructors behave normally. Another pitfall is expecting runtime errors for missing methods; in fact the compiler prevents incomplete concrete classes, catching problems earlier. This compile-time enforcement is what makes abstract classes a reliable design tool.

Let's read the Shape superclass to see how abstract classes combine concrete and abstract members. The Shape class stores a color field and provides a constructor to set it. It also implements displayColor, a concrete helper that every subclass can call. Critically, it declares calculateArea and draw as abstract methods — they have signatures but no implementation. This design forces every concrete subclass to provide a correct area calculation and a draw behavior. Notice the rule: the class contains abstract methods, so it must be declared abstract. A common learner mistake is to try to instantiate Shape; the compiler disallows it because the class is incomplete. Another oversight is to expect default behavior when a subclass forgets to override an abstract method; instead the compiler will require fixes before you can run the program. Walkthroughs like this clarify separation of responsibility: Shape shares common state and helpers while delegating geometric specifics to subclasses. Quickly review the three compact points that anchor this chapter. First, abstract classes are non-instantiable blueprints that can contain fields, constructors, concrete methods, and abstract methods. Second, an abstract method defines a required behavior without an implementation and forces concrete subclasses to implement it. Third, use abstract classes when you need both shared implementation and required, subtype-specific behavior; the compiler will catch attempts to instantiate an abstract class or to leave abstract methods unimplemented. Keep these three ideas handy as you design class hierarchies: they help you reduce duplication, express clear contracts, and rely on compile-time checks to keep behavior complete.
